subtype: Checking with someone who will say the hard thing [Response]
passage:
Subject: the honest version, please

Dear Aparna,
Thank you for last Friday. When I asked how I come across in team meetings, I was secretly hoping you'd say "confident." Instead you said I finish people's sentences and that Karan has stopped speaking up. I went home annoyed, honestly. Then I watched myself in Monday's meeting and counted: I cut in four times. Four! I had been telling myself I was just "keeping things moving."
So here's another request, and please don't soften it. I'm applying for the team lead role next month. What am I missing? What would you worry about if I got it?
You're the one person who tells me the hard thing without making me feel small. 🙏
Love,
Rukmini

qa.q: How many times did Rukmini cut in during Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Rukmini cut in four times.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini go home annoyed after Aparna's answer?
qa.a: Rukmini had been hoping to hear 'confident' and had a flattering story about 'keeping things moving', so the honest answer stung before it helped.

qa.q: What choice did Rukmini make once the sting wore off?
qa.a: Rukmini checked the feedback by counting the interruptions, then went back to Aparna with a bigger question about the team lead role, asking for it unsoftened.

qa.q: How might meetings change for Karan if Rukmini acts on this?
qa.a: Karan might start speaking up again once nobody is finishing Karan's sentences.

grounding: In an email, an adult thanks a trusted friend for honest feedback that caught a flattering blind spot and asks for more.

subtype: Checking with someone who will say the hard thing [Response]
passage: People always ask me on this show what saved the bakery. Honestly? My friend Sunaina. I'm Nandini, and two years ago I was sure everyone loved my cakes. My family said so, my cousins said so. Orders were slow, but I told myself it was the location. So one night I called Sunaina, who had worked in a restaurant kitchen for years, and said, "Please tell me what I'm not seeing. Don't be nice." She was quiet for a bit, then said, "Your cakes are lovely. But your prices change every week, and you reply to customers after two days. People think you're not serious." That stung for a whole evening. But she was right. I fixed the price list and started answering messages the same day. Orders doubled by Diwali.

qa.q: What two problems did Sunaina point out?
qa.a: Nandini's prices changed every week, and customers got replies after two days.

qa.q: Why had Nandini blamed the slow orders on the location?
qa.a: With family and cousins praising the cakes, blaming the location protected Nandini's belief that everyone loved the bakery.

qa.q: Which step made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sunaina, someone with kitchen experience, not to be nice brought out problems Nandini couldn't see, and fixing them raised the orders.

qa.q: What might it have cost Sunaina to say the hard thing?
qa.a: Sunaina risked hurting a friend, which may be why she was quiet for a bit before choosing honesty.

grounding: A bakery owner asks a friend with kitchen experience to point out what is being missed, and the honest answer corrects a flattering story.

subtype: Checking with someone who will say the hard thing [Response]
passage: Hrithik here. My flatmate Tejas had four job interviews in a row that went nowhere. For weeks he blamed the interviewers: "They wanted someone cheaper," "They'd already picked someone." Then last Sunday he put his laptop on the dining table, pressed play on a mock interview he had recorded, and said, "Watch this with me. Tell me honestly how I come across. Don't be polite." I watched. He answered every question well, but he kept saying "obviously" and rolled his eyes once at a basic question. I told him it looked a bit arrogant. He went quiet, rubbed his jaw, and then said, "Play it again." I can't say what went on in his head, but he recorded three more practice runs that evening, and there wasn't a single "obviously" in the last one.

qa.q: What did Tejas keep saying in the recorded mock interview?
qa.a: He kept saying "obviously" and rolled his eyes once at a basic question.

qa.q: Why might Tejas have blamed the interviewers for weeks?
qa.a: Blaming them protected his picture of himself as a strong candidate, so he didn't have to wonder how he was coming across.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make last Sunday, and what came of it?
qa.a: He asked Hrithik to watch the recording and be honest, then practised again until the 'obviously' disappeared.

qa.q: What might it have felt like for Hrithik to call Tejas's manner arrogant?
qa.a: Hrithik may have felt awkward saying something unflattering to a flatmate, but being asked directly made honesty possible.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man ask for blunt feedback on how he comes across, which catches what his excuses hid.

passage:
Sunday: After the team offsite, Chaitanya told himself it had gone brilliantly. He'd led every discussion. Still, two juniors had gone quiet by lunch. Over chai he asked Lalit, 'You've known me since college. How do I actually come across in meetings? Don't be polite.'
Lalit hesitated. 'You finish people's sentences. Then you say "great point" and give your own.'
Tuesday: Chaitanya was irritated for a day. Then, at the review meeting, he caught himself doing it to Shruti. He stopped mid-word. 'Sorry, go on.' Shruti finished her idea, and it was better than his.
Friday: He messaged Lalit: 'Counted today. Interrupted four times, down from I don't know how many. Keep telling me stuff like this?'
Lalit sent back: 'always 👍'

qa.q: What did Lalit say Chaitanya does in meetings?
qa.a: Chaitanya finishes people's sentences, then says 'great point' and gives his own.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel the offsite had gone brilliantly at first?
qa.a: Leading every discussion felt like success from the inside; he didn't see his interrupting, and the juniors going quiet was only a faint doubt.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Tuesday, and what did Chaitanya choose?
qa.a: Catching himself cutting Shruti off; he stopped mid-word, said 'Sorry, go on', and let her finish.

qa.q: What might it have taken for Lalit to answer honestly on Sunday?
qa.a: Lalit hesitated first, probably worried about hurting a friend; answering plainly took courage and trust that Chaitanya really wanted the truth.

grounding: An adult asks a trusted friend how he really comes across, hears a hard truth about interrupting, and uses it.

subtype: Checking with someone who will say the hard thing [Response]
passage:
Tanvir, you asked how I became a good teacher. Not by being clever. By asking Vimla.
At twenty-four, in my second year at the school in Bhubaneswar, I was sure I was the favourite. Children laughed in my class; the principal smiled at me. But the back rows' half-yearly marks were poor, and I blamed their homes.
Vimla had been my friend since hostel days, the one person who never flattered me. One evening I asked her, 'Come and sit at the back of my class tomorrow. Tell me what I'm not seeing.'
She came. Afterwards she said, 'Sudha, you asked twenty questions. Eighteen went to the first two benches. The back rows stopped raising their hands within ten minutes.'
I cried a little in the staff toilet. Then I started walking to the back of the room.
Find your Vimla, Tanvir.

qa.q: How many of Sudha's twenty questions went to the first two benches?
qa.a: Eighteen.

qa.q: Why was young Sudha so sure of being the favourite teacher?
qa.a: Laughter in class and the principal's smiles felt like proof; those flattering signs hid the back rows, whose poor marks Sudha blamed on their homes.

qa.q: What choice made the difference for Sudha, and why?
qa.a: Asking Vimla, a friend who never flattered, to sit at the back and say what Sudha was missing; an outside eye counted what Sudha couldn't see from the front.

qa.q: How might the back-row children have felt before Sudha started walking to the back of the room?
qa.a: They probably felt invisible, raising hands that were never picked until they gave up within ten minutes.

grounding: An elder recalls asking an honest friend to watch their teaching, which revealed what self-flattery had hidden.
